Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval. For $r=1,2$, $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ be such that every slice $\chi_t:U\to\chi_t(U)$ is a bijection with $C^2$ inverse and $J(t,a):=\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$, where $D_a\chi$ is the matrix of reference-coordinate partial derivatives. Write $H(t,a):=(t,\chi(t,a))$ and $\Omega:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. The map $H$ is injective and its derivative is block triangular with determinant $J>0$, so the inverse function theorem gives local $C^1$ inverses; injectivity makes them agree on overlaps. Hence $\Omega$ is open and the joint inverse $A(t,x):=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$ is $C^1$. Define $u(t,x):=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$, which is $C^1$. For any $C^1$ vector field $f$ on $\Omega$, let $D_xf$ be its matrix of spatial coordinate partial derivatives and define $D_tf:=\partial_tf+(D_xf)u$. $$SO(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}.$$

This map preserves Euclidean distances and orientation because $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$ and $\det Q=1$; the coordinate change does not assert that the observer is inertial. Define the transformed velocity, material derivative, rate tensors and acceleration from $\chi^*$ by the same formulas on $\Omega^*$; in particular, $D_t^*f=\partial_tf+(D_{x^*}f)u^*$ and $a_m^*:=D_t^*u^*$. $$u^*(t,x^*)=Q'(t)x+Q(t)u(t,x)+c'(t),\qquad L^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)L(t,x)Q(t)^{\mathsf T}+Q'(t)Q(t)^{\mathsf T},$$

$$D^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)D(t,x)Q(t)^{\mathsf T},\qquad W^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)W(t,x)Q(t)^{\mathsf T}+Q'(t)Q(t)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \theta^*(t,x^*)=\theta(t,x).$$

$$a_m^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)a_m(t,x)+2Q'(t)u(t,x)+Q''(t)x+c''(t).$$

derivations.claim: By the velocity-gradient convention [F1], in the original observer $L=\nabla u=\Omega$, so the candidate response is $\tau=\mu\Omega\ne0$. Define $Q(t)=\exp(-\Omega t)$. The matrix-exponential power series and $\Omega^T=-\Omega$ give $Q'=-\Omega Q=-Q\Omega$, $Q^T=Q^{-1}$, and $Q(0)=I_3$. The matrix $Q(t)$ is continuous and orthogonal, so $\det Q(t)\in\{-1,1\}$ is continuous; since $I=\mathbb R$ is connected and $\det Q(0)=1$, $\det Q(t)=1$ for all $t$. Thus $Q(t)\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$.
Take the rigid observer $x^*=Q(t)x$, $c=0$. By [F2], its velocity is $u^*=Qu+Q'x=Q\Omega x-\Omega Qx=0$, because $Q\Omega=\Omega Q$. Thus $L^*=0$ and the same candidate law gives $\tau^*=0$.

Objectivity from [F1] would instead require $\tau^*=Q\tau Q^T=\mu Q\Omega Q^T=\mu\Omega\ne0$, since $Q$ commutes with $\Omega$. This contradicts step 2.1, so the candidate $\tau=\mu L$ is not objective. The example tests a tensor law and makes no claim that it satisfies a separate angular-momentum or empirical admissibility condition.

citations.quote: Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a closed nondegenerate rectangle, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its graph has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.
A bounded real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable if and only if its discontinuity set is null.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its indicator $1_E$ is Riemann integrable on a fixed nondegenerate bounding
rectangle $Q$. In that case
$$\int_Q1_E=\operatorname{cont}(E).$$

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Put $S=\partial V$. It is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F4]. At each $p\in S$, the local graph condition gives rigid coordinates and an open planar set on which $S$ is the graph of a $C^1$ function. Choose a small closed nondegenerate rectangle inside that planar set so its graph lies within the boundary chart and covers a neighborhood of $p$ in $S$. Compactness gives finitely many such graph patches covering $S$. Each patch has content zero by [F1]. A rigid image of a cube of side $\ell$ lies in an axis-parallel cube of side $\sqrt3\ell$, so rigid coordinate changes enlarge the total covering volume by at most $3\sqrt3$. Thus each patch has content zero in the original coordinates.

Parameterize a local graph patch at $p\in S$ by $\gamma(y)=(y,h(y))$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$; its derivative has rank two because its first two coordinates are $y$. Differentiate $\phi^{-1}\circ\phi=\mathrm{id}$ and use [F11] to see that $D\phi$ is invertible. Thus $D(\phi\circ\gamma)$ has rank two. Choose rigid target coordinates so the first two coordinates of this derivative are invertible. The inverse function theorem [F10] gives a local $C^1$ inverse for those two coordinates, so the third coordinate expresses $\phi(S)$ locally as a $C^1$ graph. The homeomorphism $\phi$ maps the local one-sided region $V$ to one side of that image graph. Hence $\phi(V)$ has locally $C^1$ graph boundary.
By [F2], the finite union of the source graph patches in step 1.1 shows that $S$ has content zero.

The compact image $\phi(S)$ has a finite cover by the local graph patches from step 1.2. Let $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $V$ lying locally on one side of that graph. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline V\subset U$. Let $\phi:U\to\phi(U)$ be a bijection onto an open image with $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ both $C^1$, and let $f:\phi(U)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator is Riemann integrable by the zero-extension convention; a set has content zero when it has finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume. Then $V$ and $\phi(V)$ are bounded open sets with locally $C^1$ graph boundaries, their compact closures are Jordan measurable, $\partial V$ and $\phi(\partial V)$ have content zero, and

$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its indicator $1_E$ is Riemann integrable on a fixed nondegenerate bounding
rectangle $Q$. In that case
$$\int_Q1_E=\operatorname{cont}(E).$$

derivations.claim: If $h(a_0)>0$ at some $a_0\in\Omega$, continuity gives a closed ball $\overline{B_r(a_0)}\subset\Omega$ and a constant $c>0$ with $h\ge c$ on that ball. Let $V=B_r(a_0)$. At each sphere point $p$, choose rigid coordinates centered at $a_0$ with the third axis parallel to $p-a_0$. Near $p$, the sphere is the graph $z=\sqrt{r^2-|y|^2}$ over a disk about $y=0$ (reversing the third axis if needed), and $V$ lies on one side; hence $V$ is a bounded $C^1$ subdomain. Choose a nondegenerate closed cube $Q\subset V$. By [F1] the integral over $V$ exists; monotonicity [F2] and the cube-content formula [F3] give $\int_V1\,dx\ge\int_Q1\,dx=\operatorname{vol}(Q)>0$, hence $\int_Vh\,dx\ge c\int_V1\,dx>0$. This contradicts the zero-integral hypothesis. If instead $h(a_0)<0$, the same ball construction gives $h\le-c$ on $V$ and $\int_Vh\,dx\le-c\int_V1\,dx<0$, contradicting either stated integral hypothesis.

The zero-integral case therefore has neither positive nor negative values, so $h=0$ throughout $\Omega$. The nonnegative-integral case has no negative values, so $h\ge0$ throughout $\Omega$. These are the two asserted conclusions.
